demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
I can't deal with even the slightest upset

issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, helicopter or aircraft sounds imply a very specific accident/emergency context that is unsupported by the rest of the profile. With no matching accident-related memory or appraisal content, this trigger is hard to reconcile with the described trauma.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: This trigger suggests a road traffic crash scenario, but the rest of the profile does not indicate the loved one died in a vehicle accident. In the absence of congruent memory or appraisal items, it appears mismatched to the trauma narrative.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: A betrayal appraisal is difficult to integrate with an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one when the other selected items center on fragmented reliving and self-blame/capability loss rather than interpersonal wrongdoing. This appraisal points to a different trauma meaning than the rest of the profile.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile there is no corresponding trauma-linked content in Memory or Appraisals to explain why this specific cue would be prominent. The rest of the profile centers on fragmented grief-trauma memory and self-blame/capability concerns, making this trigger feel clinically unanchored.

A burnt smell suggests a fire/burning danger context, but neither the trauma type nor the selected Memory and Appraisal items indicate a death scenario involving fire, destruction, or sensory danger cues. This creates a hard-to-explain mismatch across nodes.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after a loved one's death, but here it is not supported by any memory content suggesting perceived responsibility, preventability, or a specific action/inaction. Combined with sensory triggers implying unrelated contexts, this appraisal lacks a coherent link to the rest of the profile.

For traumatic bereavement, baby sounds are not impossible, but with the rest of the profile they stand out as poorly anchored. The memory items describe intrusive, fragmented reliving of the death, yet there is no linked appraisal or other trigger content suggesting children, parenting, hospital maternity contexts, or infant-related aspects of the loss. This makes the trigger hard to connect clinically to the stated trauma and formulation.

Car sounds imply a road-traffic context for the death, but no other selected item supports that context. The memory and appraisal items are generic and do not reflect accident-related meaning, danger, guilt, or sensory links. As chosen, this trigger appears insufficiently integrated with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: This trigger is plausible in bereavement, but in this profile it points toward loss-related meanings about absence and foreshortened future, whereas the negative appraisals instead focus on generalized personal weakness and incapacity. The trigger content and appraisal content therefore do not cohere well.

issues.item: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: This appraisal is more characteristic of trauma involving personal failure, injury, or loss of role capacity. In an unexpected death profile, it could occur, but here it is not supported by the trigger or memory content, which centers on reliving and fragmentation rather than role loss. The item feels mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
issues.explanation: This suggests ongoing decision-related mistrust or guilt/responsibility themes, but the rest of the profile does not include cues of responsibility for the loved one’s death, moral injury, or repeated choice points. Without supporting memory or trigger content, this appraisal is weakly coherent.

issues.item: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person
issues.explanation: This is not impossible, but together with the other appraisal items it creates a self-concept dominated by incompetence/weakness, while the triggers are largely sensory/future-oriented and the memory items are classic reliving/disorganization phenomena. The appraisal theme is not well linked to the selected trauma cues and memory content.

vignette:
Arjun Patel was 53 when his partner’s adult son was shot and killed outside a neighborhood liquor store. He had driven the young man there after an argument earlier that evening, one of those tense, ordinary family exchanges that now felt to Arjun like the hinge on which everything turned. He remembered the sour alcohol smell on the sidewalk near the entrance, the faint burnt odor drifting from somewhere behind the strip mall, and then the crack of gunfire that split the parking lot. After that, the scene no longer existed in his mind as a single sequence. What remained were jagged fragments: the young man turning, a bottle breaking, people shouting, his own hands shaking on the steering wheel. Other parts would not come at all, no matter how hard he tried to force them back, and what he did have did not feel like a memory from the past. It came at him as if it were happening again.

In the months that followed, Arjun became convinced that the death had happened because of the way he had acted. He believed he should not have driven him there, should have stopped the argument differently, should have known something bad would happen. That self-blame seemed to fasten itself onto the worst pieces of the night, pulling them repeatedly into the foreground while leaving the rest stubbornly blank. He would lie awake trying to reconstruct the missing minutes, certain that if he could remember them properly he would finally see the exact moment he had failed. Instead, the memory broke apart further under pressure, returning as flashes that felt immediate and unfinished.

His work as a cybersecurity analyst had once suited him because of its predictability, but even the office began to feel dangerous in oddly specific ways. If a coworker came back from lunch smelling of alcohol, Arjun’s body reacted before he could think; the odor seemed to yank him straight back to the liquor store, and the scene arrived with the force of the present tense. If something in the office kitchen scorched and sent out a burnt smell, he would stop mid-task, heart racing, caught in disconnected sensory shards of that night. Sudden sharp noises—a dropped metal cart in the hallway, a construction bang outside the building—hit him like gunshots. He was not simply reminded; for a few moments he was there again, with no reliable bridge between then and now.

What frightened Arjun most was not only the memory itself but what it seemed to say about him. Because he had come to believe he had caused the death through his own failure, each involuntary return of the scene hardened his conviction that he was dangerous and fundamentally unable to cope. The gaps in recall did not reassure him; they made him suspect there was something even worse in the missing pieces, some proof of negligence or cowardice still hidden from him. He also became afraid of his own anger. Startled by a loud crack or overcome by the smell of alcohol, he could feel a surge of heat and tension that he interpreted as the beginning of losing control. He was certain that if he let himself get fully angry, he might do something terrible.

That fear changed how he moved through his days. He began scanning constantly for the cues that might set him off: who in the elevator smelled like whiskey, whether the break room carried a burnt odor, whether a sound outside might become another shot. Because he believed he could not handle even minor upset, he treated these sensations as warnings of collapse. The more he watched for them, the more often he found them, and each encounter brought back the fragmented, present-tense memory with fresh force. In turn, those intrusive fragments seemed to confirm that he was as unstable as he feared. At work he started keeping his office door shut and wearing headphones, not for concentration but to muffle sudden sounds. He took the stairs to avoid close quarters with people whose breath might carry alcohol. His performance slipped because so much of his attention was spent bracing for the next sensory ambush rather than tracking threats on a screen.

At home, his partner experienced him as distant and easily agitated. Arjun withdrew from dinners out and refused errands that might take him near the strip mall where the shooting happened. When his partner lit something on the stove by accident one evening and the kitchen filled briefly with a burnt smell, Arjun snapped, then immediately recoiled in shame, reading the incident as evidence that his anger was becoming dangerous. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of holding himself together. He said he no longer trusted his own mind: the memory came in pieces, the pieces felt current, and every trigger seemed to prove he was one moment away from either breaking down or lashing out. What he wanted most was to know whether the night could ever feel truly over, and what he feared most was discovering that it never would.
